validation is an essential part of the development of any new measurement method, whereas verification is needed for the use of a method in its intended environment.
the use of harmonised procedures is essential for the validation and verification of bioanalytical methods, and that these should be performed in accordance with a fitness-for-purpose evaluation.

validation procedures in clinical chemistry are not yet sufficiently standardized, harmonized or internationally accepted to be generally applicable in the field of clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine.
there is still a need for a harmonized approach to validation and verification in clinical chemistry, but that the current state of the art is sufficient for most purposes.
validation and verification of bioanalysis methods is a process that should be performed by the manufacturer, the end-user, or both in order to achieve a satisfactory overall measurement quality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the present validation and verification procedures for measurement methods in clinical biochemistry are generally satisfactory.
validation is an important tool in bioanalysis, but it cannot replace the verification in the end-users' laboratory.
we have a long way to go before we have a generally accepted and harmonized system for validation and verification procedures for all methods used in bioanalysis, but we are on the right track.

validation is a process that should start with a thorough fitness-for-purpose analysis and that the validation procedures are best performed by an independent third party.
the use of harmonization concepts, fitness-for-purpose and uncertainty of measurements is the most efficient way to ensure the quality of measurement methods in bioanalysis.
